title: Malawi govt axes 298 ‘ghost teachers’ from payroll in massive crackdown as officials hunt for civil service fraudsters
text_paragraph_1: Malawi’s government has struck a major blow in its war against payroll fraud, sensationally removing 298 teachers from the September 2026 payroll after they failed to show up for a crucial nationwide verification exercise designed to root out so-called “ghost workers”.
text_paragraph_2: The Department of Human Resource Management and Development revealed the dramatic purge as part of an ongoing, months-long personnel audit targeting civil servants across the country, aimed squarely at exposing fraudsters siphoning off taxpayer money through fictitious or unverified employment records.
text_paragraph_3: According to an explosive letter from the Ministry of Education, signed by Norah Chikhungu on behalf of the Secretary for Education, the 298 teachers and officers were unceremoniously struck off the payroll after failing to undergo the mandatory verification process.

text_paragraph_2: In her first year at St. Michaels Girls Secondary School in Mangochi, Malawi, Joyce Chisale got the highest marks in everything from Chichewa language classes to biology and history. But her parents had trouble keeping up with payments; the boarding school's annual fees were roughly half her father's yearly salary, and there were three other siblings to support.
text_paragraph_3: That might have meant the abrupt end of Joyce's formal education and her dreams of becoming a doctor or scientist. Then The K.I.N.D. text_paragraph_1: The Controller and Accountant-General’s Department (CAGD), in its statement dated 27 September 2026, has provided an important clarification on the ongoing controversy over the placement of promoted teachers and the payment of their salary arrears. CAGD states that it received 6,079 completed promotion cases from the Ghana Education Service out of an expected 58,620 cases, and that all 6,079 cases submitted had been processed and paid, including applicable arrears, in the September 2026 salaries.
text_paragraph_2: This disclosure raises serious questions for the Ghana Education Service (GES). If 58,620 cases were expected but only 6,079 had been submitted to CAGD as of 22 September, what has happened to the remaining cases? Why have thousands of teachers who have earned promotions not yet been placed on their appropriate salary scales? What steps has GES taken to complete and submit the outstanding documentation to CAGD?
text_paragraph_3: These questions cannot be answered through silence. GES must account to the teachers it employs and to the public.
